You're listening to K S P X, ninety eight point one F M. It's a beautiful morning in the valley.
This hour, we're talking about how F M radio works, and why your car radio sounds so clear.
F M stands for frequency modulation. Instead of changing how strong the signal is, the station wiggles its frequency in step with the sound.
Static from lightning mostly changes signal strength, so it barely bothers F M.
Each station gets a channel about two hundred kilohertz wide. On a waterfall display, that's the wide, bright stripe.
That's K S P X, ninety eight point one. Stay with us.
This is K V L Y, ninety eight point seven. Here's your weather: sunny and mild, with highs near seventy two.
On the community calendar, the amateur radio club is offering a free license class Saturday at the library. No experience needed.
The technician exam has thirty five questions. You need twenty six correct to pass.
Traffic is light on the freeway this morning. You're listening to K V L Y, ninety eight point seven.
Welcome back to Radio Science Minute, on K Q R D, ninety eight point nine.
Today's question: why do A M stations travel farther at night?
After sunset, the lowest layer of the ionosphere fades away. That lets medium wave signals bounce off higher layers, and skip hundreds of miles.
That's called sky wave propagation. Now you know. This is K Q R D, ninety eight point nine.
